catalog_quote: 2.3.2.1 Segmental features In Pangkhua, a phonological word must be minimally bimoraic . A phonological word must have at least one primary stress and only bimoraic or relatively heavier syllables can receive a primary stress . Thus, the bimoraic words ranging from (a) - (d) tend to attract stress . On the other hand, monomoraic or relatively lighter syllables (that typi- cally have only a short vowel ə ranging from (e) - (f) tend not to attract stress . Bimoraic or bigger syllables: " a . With an onset pa [ px] ' ', ' father ' where the long vowel makes two moras . b . With a coda: in [ ? in], ' drink ' where the long vowel and the coda makes three ... 2.3.2.2 Prosodic features In Pangkhua, a phonological word must have at least one primary stress . ... [p. 73] ... can head a phonological word hosting a primary stressed syllable, while affixes and clitics cannot do so . ... [beside Table 51] this nominalizer may have undergone reductions (a > ə) in Pangkhua's predominantly iambic feet . ... [HL overview §5, p. 8, sesquisyllables:] The major syllable that carries the tonal properties and prosodic prominence is always word final. The reduction of the non-final vowel in the first syllable and the prosodic prominence of the word-final syllable makes this type of words a disyllabic iamb.

new_statements.quote: Pangkhua is a quantity sensitive language. Basic syllables can be light or heavy, depending on whether or not there is a final X [...] [§5] Pangkhua has a set of words with sesquisyllabic structure. This word-type consists of a final heavy syllable preceded by a light and phonologically reduced first syllable. The major syllable that carries the tonal properties and prosodic prominence is always word final. The reduction of the non-final vowel in the first syllable and the prosodic prominence of the word-final syllable makes this type of words a disyllabic iamb.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Pangkhua has two lexical tones (H, L; low functional load). The only explicit prominence statement concerns sesquisyllabic words (reduced light presyllable + heavy final syllable, ~127 items): prominence and tone sit on the word-final major syllable, i.e. an iambic (final-prominent) disyllable. The author also calls the language quantity-sensitive (light vs heavy syllables) but gives no general rule locating stress in ordinary polysyllabic/multisyllabic roots, prefixed roots or compounds in this overview.
new_statements.exceptions: None; statement is restricted to the sesquisyllabic word type. Löffler 1985 adds only that prefixes are toneless/unmarked and high-toned syllables are longer.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (lexical word types); scope limited to sesquisyllables. The full treatment is in Akter 2024 A Grammar of Pangkhua §2.2.5 Sesquisyllable (p. 51) and §2.3.2 Phonological word (pp. 63-70), not accessible here; those sections may contain a general stress criterion for the phonological word and would supersede this.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Pangkhua as spoken in Pangkhua Para (Dinthar) village, Bilaichari, Rangamati district, Chittagong Hill Tracts, Bangladesh (Akter's fieldwork 2017-2020); Löffler 1985 calls it 'Paang(khua)'. Same language as Glottolog pank1249 / ISO pkh; Indian and Myanmar populations not described.

sources.locator: §5 'Sesquisyllabicity', printed p. 8 (p. 9); with §4 p. 7 and §3.1.3 pp. 6-7 on quantity and tone
sources.note: No general word-stress rule. §3.1.3: two lexical tones (H realized mid-level, L low-falling), 'comparatively low functional load'. §4 p.7: 'Pangkhua is a quantity sensitive language' (light vs heavy syllables). §5 p.8: in sesquisyllabic words the major syllable carrying tone and prosodic prominence is always word-final; such words are 'a disyllabic iamb'. Refers to Akter (2022: 76-82) for acoustics of tone.

sources.note: Derivative (OT phonotactics on an online corpus, relies on Akter 2024). p.144: sesquisyllabic patterns 'where a minor syllable (with a reduced vowel or consonant) precedes a stressed main syllable'; explicitly leaves 'acoustic studies of tone and stress' to future research. No word-stress rule.

sources.note: Nothing on stress. pp. 279-280: initials, vowels/finals as in Lushai; two main tones (high, low) plus three 'secondary tones' (emphatic, high allotone, high-falling in exclamations); prefixes left unmarked for tone; high-toned syllables longer; downstep-like lowering of H to mid in non-initial position.
